#Please note: This situation has been resolved already. I am no longer worried about this issue. Feel free to add your two cents if you want, but please keep that in mind.

Spring and summer are when cycling is most popular for obvious reasons, and consequently this is when bike theft peaks as well. For this reason, I'm getting a 20" wheel folding bike. A folding bike will allow me to take my bike inside instead of leaving it locked outside. In this way, I will not have to worry about my bike being stolen during the peak months of the year... and I won't have to carry a heavy lock everywhere I go in town.

One of the things I will be using the folding bike for is to go grocery shopping, and one thing I think you definitely don't want to do is ride a bicycle while wearing a heavily weighed down backpack. It's awkward, it's sweaty, and it hurts. That's why you normally want to carry as much as you can on the bike itself. You want to either fasten your stuff to a rack, or store it inside some bags clipped to the sides of that rack. Fine. Good. But what if that's not much of an option?

The bike will definitely have a rack. I may even add an extra rack on the front depending on whether it interferes with the fold or not. Even still, I highly doubt I will be able to fit full size panniers on either rack. I do have a smaller set of bags which I know will fit, so I'll probably be using those, but I don't know if they will interfere with the bike's fold when the bags are empty. If they do, I may have to ditch the bags and wear a backpack instead.

But backpacks suck on a bike, especially when loaded with 20 pounds of groceries. Please advise me. Maybe there is something I am overlooking, or maybe there is some amazing backpack that doesn't suck to ride with when it's heavily loaded up.

----------

**edit:**. I think I have a possible solution. Given the unusual geometry of a folding bike, I might be able to simply hang a backpack over the front handlebars. I vaguely recall actually having seen people do this before. It may even be better for the bike's overall balance... but I'd have to make sure that the backpack is fairly stable like this. I can't have it swinging around independently of the handlebars, because that would make steering difficult. Any advice on accomplishing this would be appreciated.

**edit2:** Yeah, it looks like it may be a viable solution. I found a video of a guy touring through china with his backpack hooked over the handlebars and resting on the top of bike's tube.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vxJRfPhXWOU

If it's stable enough for him, then with a little experimenting, maybe it'll work for me too. I'm just worried about hitting my knees on it when pedaling, but he doesn't mention that as an issue and his bike looks fairly short in length. Hmmmmm...

----------

**edit 3:** It turns out the bike actually has a special set of threaded holes on the outside of the head tube where a quick detach bracket can be installed. There are several different things one can attach to the bracket, including a large rack, a large bag, or a basket. All I need to do is order one, and I should be set for hauling weight at the front of the bike where it will help keep weight more evenly distributed. And since it's on the head tube instead of the handlebars, people say it doesn't affect the steering.

I also was able to fit a set of panniers onto the rear rack. They just *barely* fit without causing heel strike, but I won't know that for certain until I go for my first ride. So, despite this being a folding bike, things seem to be looking up in terms of carrying capacity, which is good, because I will be using the bike for shopping.

Lastly, I was able to re-purpose an old small brake-mounted front rack that doesn't interfere with the bike's fold! It's a cheap rack that's not designed for panniers though, and it's not at all sturdy, but it will definitely be put to good use until I get my hands on that special bracket. ????
I need advice. Cycling with a backpack?

Dutchie here, and I always carry groceries in a daypack (35L) or shoulder bag (10L).

It really depends on how far you've got to ride, and how often you can go to the store. I've got stores all around me, and the most I'm willing to take regularly is 7-8 kilos (15-18 pounds) for about 20 minutes. I do however spread my shopping, so I go more frequently if I've got a lot of stuff to get.

As far as backpacks go, get one that fits well. With a supporting frame, and maybe with a hip- and chestbelt. I find hiking bags way more comfortable than any kind of fashionable bag. FWIW, I use an Ortovox Thunder.

The shortest distance I have to bike to my nearest, least favorite grocery store is about 6 miles. I usually go nearly 7.5 miles to my most favorite store. Along that route is some serious hill climbing in both directions. I can go the long way around, and sometimes I do, but it adds a few miles. It's also a much less safe route and doesn't reduce the hill climbing by that much. I go grocery shopping roughly every other day of the week, and sometimes daily.

My trips are long enough to safely say that carrying weight comfortably is important. I can't get away with a backpack that is going to unbalance my torso when loaded and cause any strain or discomfort at all, because it's going to add up.

Do you use a city or a road bike? With a city bike carrying is easier, as with a road bike Your backpack has to follow the arch from your back. A bp without a frame may be more practical in that case.

As the OP says, it will be a folding bike with 20" wheels. Did you not read it?

I normally use a touring bike with the capability to hold a full set of front and rear panniers. Carrying stuff is not an issue at all on that bike. It's the folding bike I'm worried about.
No need to get snarky, I forgot about that.

I regularly bike with a backpack to buy my groceries(anywhere from 1-5 miles). Often have potatoes too, so 20lbs easily. I use a light trail bag with no frame to hold my cold stuff( throw an ice bag in there pre-trip). Works for me, but if you don't want a sweaty back, the rack is a better way to go, just make sure you strap/secure everything.There is also "basket bags" that tie to handlebars you might like, which also distributes some weight to the front, which-in turn- helps out the load on your bike.

I've tried a quick detach handlebar basket on one of my other bikes. It's not so great. The basket holds a lot less stuff than you think it will, and stuff can fly out if you hit a bump. Both of these problems can be solved somewhat with a cargo net stretched over the mouth of the basket, but a basket still isn't going to be able to hold as much weight as I'd like. Still, it's an option worth considering when combined with a rear rack and possibly a set of panniers, especially since the fact that it can detach means that it won't interfere with folding the bike.

Handlebar bag on a folding bike? No thanks. Too much hassle taking it off and putting it back on just to be able to fold the bike.

Ortlieb has lockable, quick release handlebar bags. Some of the Tern folding bikes have these integrated into the handlebars.

http://www.ucycle.com/product/ortlieb-ultimate6-m-classic-187499-1.htm

Yes, I know about those specific bags from ortlieb. They're also compatible with klickfix. I have one from topeak on my touring bike (it's not klickfix compatible though). With a folding bike, these bags are best used with a special attachment that goes on the front of the bike frame, not the handlebars. That is the absolute worst place to put a bag on a folder. The bracket gets in the way, and it affects the steering, which is already a bit twitchy. Several manufacturers have an option for a frame mountable quick release bracket, including tern, dahon, and brompton. This is where bags should go.
